attack_steps.name: Exploit Public-Facing Application as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The Fire Chili rootkit is characterized by a multi-stage infection process involving a dropper, a loader (newdev.dll), and a final payload (Milestone backdoor).  Themida, a software packer designed to obfuscate code and hinder reverse engineering analysis, is utilized by the malware for protection. Network evasion techniques are employed by Fire Chili to conceal network connections from detection tools such as netstat through the interception and modification of system calls related to network information.

The deployment of Fire Chili is believed to have been facilitated following the exploitation of the Log4j vulnerability (CVE-2021-44228). This critical vulnerability in the widely used Java logging library, Log4j, permitted attackers to execute arbitrary code on vulnerable systems through specially crafted input.  

Initial access to target systems is likely achieved by exploiting this Log4j vulnerability. Attackers would have sent malicious payloads disguised as legitimate data to servers running vulnerable Log4j applications.

attack_steps.name: Command and Scripting Interpreter: Windows Command Shell as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The Windows Command Shell (cmd.exe) is frequently exploited by malware due to its capabilities for executing commands on a system.  Malware often injects its own code into running cmd.exe processes or initiates new ones, enabling command execution without user interface interaction.

Within cmd.exe, malware can execute valid Windows commands, encompassing file manipulation, system configuration alterations, network communication establishment, and process control functionalities. 

Obfuscation techniques are frequently employed by malware authors to conceal the commands sent to cmd.exe, hindering detection and analysis by security tools.  


System-level access granted to cmd.exe poses a significant security risk, enabling malware to make profound changes to a system. The stealthy nature of obfuscated commands can mask malicious activity from users and security tools. Furthermore, malware can leverage cmd.exe for lateral movement across networks.

mitre_technique.name: Command and scripting interpreter: windows command shell
mitre_technique.description: Adversaries may abuse the Windows command shell for execution. The Windows command shell (cmd) is the primary command prompt on Windows systems. The Windows command prompt can be used to control almost any aspect of a system, with various permission levels required for different subsets of commands. The command prompt can be invoked remotely via Remote Services such as SSH.

pre-conditions:

The malware has the capability to execute code.

A Windows operating system is present.

attack_steps.name: System Services: Service Execution as used by the malware
attack_steps.description: The "COLDFIRE" malware exploits the System Services: Service Execution technique to achieve persistent and stealthy operation within compromised systems.  A new Windows service is likely created by the malware, potentially employing a legitimate-sounding name to evade detection. Malicious code is then injected into this newly established service. Upon configuration, the service is automatically initiated and executed as a background process by the operating system. Due to the inherent trust bestowed upon services within the Windows architecture, they frequently operate with elevated privileges. This grants the injected malicious code increased control over the system resources.

The Windows service control manager (services.exe) is an interface to manage and manipulate services. The service control manager is accessible to users via GUI components as well as system utilities such as sc.exe and Net.

attack_steps.name: Create or Modify System Process: Windows Service as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
The Fire Chili rootkit is characterized by its multifaceted capabilities designed to evade detection. Persistence is achieved through the creation of a Windows service designated as "msupdate2" or variations thereof, ensuring continuous operation even after system reboots.

Process hiding techniques are employed to obscure malicious processes from standard monitoring tools such as Task Manager. This is accomplished by intercepting system calls related to process management and manipulating data structures to remove entries corresponding to malicious processes from viewable lists.

Network connection obfuscation is achieved through the interception of network-related IOCTLs (Input/Output Control) sent to the system. Connections matching predefined criteria associated with the malware are filtered out, hindering detection by security tools.

File system manipulation capabilities are attributed to the rootkit, although specific methods remain undisclosed. It is suggested that the rootkit may alter file attributes or content to evade detection by antivirus software.

Technical details reveal the utilization of a dropper program that downloads and executes a loader module named "newdev.dll." This loader subsequently decrypts and loads a backdoor component known as "Milestone," which is based on the Gh0st RAT framework.

Communication between the Milestone backdoor and a command-and-control (C2) server occurs uncompressed, differing from some other variants of Gh0st RAT.

Analysis indicates the existence of diverse Fire Chili versions, including those derived from leaked Gh0st RAT source code. Potential links to the Deep Panda threat actor group are suggested due to similarities in employed techniques.


The sophisticated nature of Fire Chili underscores the continuous evolution of malware tactics. Its ability to conceal processes, obfuscate network traffic, and establish persistent presence on infected systems presents significant challenges for detection and removal.

mitre_technique.name: Create or modify system process: windows service
mitre_technique.description: Adversaries may create or modify Windows services to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. When Windows boots up, it starts programs or applications called services that perform background system functions. Windows service configuration information, including the file path to the service's executable or recovery programs/commands, is stored in the Windows Registry.

pre-conditions:
The system has a running instance of the Windows operating system.

The user account executing the process has sufficient privileges to create and modify system services.

attack_steps.name: Obfuscated Files or Information: Software Packing as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
Software packing techniques, specifically employing Themida, are utilized by the Milestone2017 variants of COLDSTEEL malware to facilitate defense evasion.  

Themida, a commercial software protection tool, is frequently leveraged by malware authors due to its robust encryption algorithms, code virtualization capabilities, and integrated anti-debugging features. These attributes contribute to the obfuscation of malicious code, rendering it more difficult for security analysis tools to identify and interpret its functionality. 

The packing process involves the compilation of original COLDSTEEL source code, followed by input into Themida.  Subsequently, encryption and compression are applied to the code, resulting in a significantly reduced and less readable form. The code's structure is also rewritten, introducing additional layers of complexity. A stub program is generated as part of this process. This stub functions as a loader, responsible for decrypting and decompressing the packed code upon malware execution.

The application of Themida within COLDSTEEL (Milestone2017) presents significant challenges to security analysis efforts. The heavily encrypted and obfuscated nature of the packed code hinders the identification of malicious intent and functionality by researchers.  Furthermore, traditional antivirus signatures, which often rely on recognizing specific code patterns, are rendered less effective due to the dynamic nature of packed code resulting from the packing process.


The consequences of employing Themida in COLDSTEEL (Milestone2017) are substantial. The malware's ability to evade detection and analysis is significantly enhanced, enabling attackers to:

- Spread undetected within systems, avoiding triggering alarms or raising suspicion.
- Execute malicious activities once inside a system, such as data theft, installation of additional malware, or operational disruption.

attack_steps.name: Modify Registry as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
Registry key modifications are frequently employed by malware for several purposes. These modifications can be implemented to ensure persistence by enabling automatic execution upon system startup. Additionally, malware may alter file and process names or descriptions to evade detection.  Malicious code can also be stored within registry values for subsequent execution.

In specific instances, malware modifies registry keys directly to append a description to its service. This practice is likely undertaken for two primary reasons: disguise and evasion. By assigning a seemingly legitimate name or description to its service, malware attempts to assimilate with other system services and minimize suspicion. Furthermore, modifying the description may assist malware in evading detection by security tools that scrutinize unusual or suspicious registry changes.

Registry modifications constitute a prevalent tactic utilized by malware, presenting significant challenges for detection and removal. The inherent nature of the registry, as the central component of Windows governing numerous system settings and processes, grants malware with extensive access upon modification. Malicious alterations can be subtle and difficult to discern without specialized tools. Moreover, persistence is often ensured through registry modifications, enabling malware to continue operation even after system restarts.

To mitigate the risks associated with malware that modifies the registry, several protective measures can be implemented.  Maintaining an updated system is crucial as security updates frequently address vulnerabilities exploited by malware. Employing robust antivirus software capable of detecting and removing malware, including those targeting the registry, is essential. Exercise caution when downloading software, ensuring it originates from trusted sources. Regularly backing up data provides a safeguard against potential malware infection, enabling system restoration if necessary.

attack_steps.name: Indicator Removal: File Deletion as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
File deletion is a capability exhibited by the COLDSTEEL malware.  The precise mechanism employed for file deletion remains unspecified; however, inferences can be drawn regarding its potential methodologies.

Direct file system manipulation through system calls or API functions is a plausible method. Such functions could include DeleteFile or analogous operations contingent upon the operating system in use. Alternatively, scripting languages such as PowerShell might be leveraged by COLDSTEEL to execute commands for file deletion. This approach could facilitate more intricate scenarios, encompassing the deletion of files based on predefined patterns or criteria.

Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) associated with this capability include the presence of specific deleted filenames, such as "1.bat", "syn.exe", and "1.dll".  Furthermore, system logs may contain entries documenting file deletion events, potentially correlating timestamps and process names to COLDSTEEL activity.

Mitigation strategies encompass the implementation of regular data backups to facilitate recovery even in the event of malicious file deletion. Robust antivirus and endpoint security solutions can contribute to the detection and prevention of such activities.  User education programs aimed at fostering awareness regarding suspicious files and links can serve to reduce the risk of infection.

attack_steps.name: System Information Discovery as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
System information discovery techniques employed by the COLDSTEEL malware are inferred through analysis of common methodologies utilized by similar malicious software.  

These techniques may include direct API calls to retrieve system-level data such as computer name, operating system details, processor architecture, memory availability, and process information. 

Furthermore, COLDSTEEL is likely to conduct registry scans to extract user account credentials, installed software inventories, network configurations, and system settings. Network information, including interface details, IP addresses, and MAC addresses, may be gathered using APIs such as GetAdaptersInfo.  

File system access could enable the malware to identify sensitive documents, configuration files, and logs containing valuable data. 


The specific techniques employed by COLDSTEEL may exhibit variations contingent upon its objectives and the characteristics of the target environment.

attack_steps.name: File and Directory Discovery as used by the malware

Network communication via raw TCP connections to a Command and Control (C2) server suggests the possibility of exfiltrating gathered file and directory information.  The application of obfuscation techniques complicates the precise determination of COLDSTEEL's file discovery methodologies.

attack_steps.name: Non-Application Layer Protocol as used by the malware
attack_steps.description:
COLDSTEEL utilizes the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) for communication with its command-and-control (C2) server.  A TCP socket is established on the infected machine to facilitate this interaction. Connection establishment involves a SYN packet sent by COLDSTEEL to the C2 server, followed by a SYN-ACK response from the server. Data exchange occurs through custom messages transmitted over the established TCP connection.

The structure of these messages typically comprises a header and a payload. The header contains a command ID, indicating the type of command being executed, and a message length field specifying the total message size.  A parameter field may be present for future extensions or variations in command execution. The payload carries the data associated with the command, which can include system information, file paths, or command arguments.

To hinder detection, COLDSTEEL likely employs obfuscation and encryption techniques such as XOR encryption using a shared secret key and encoding schemes like base64.

mitre_technique.name: Non-application layer protocol

The list of possible protocols is extensive. Specific examples include use of network layer protocols, such as the Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP), transport layer protocols, such as the User Datagram Protocol (UDP), session layer protocols, such as Socket Secure (SOCKS), as well as redirected/tunneled protocols, such as Serial over LAN (SOL).
